core: What phishing is: a deceptive message impersonating a trusted party to obtain credentials or money or to deliver malware
Phishing as a form of social engineering (manipulating people, not defeating technical controls)

How to recognize it: red flags per CISA and FTC (urgency/threats, requests for credentials or payment, mismatched or shortened links, lookalike/spoofed sender addresses, generic greetings, unexpected attachments or fake invoices, too-good-to-be-true offers)
The caution that AI now produces polished, error-free phishing, so good grammar is not proof of legitimacy
Variants by targeting: spear phishing (targeted) and whaling (executives)
Variants by channel: smishing (SMS/text) and vishing (voice)
What to do: don't click/reply, verify through an independently known channel, report (company, IT, FTC), delete
MFA limits damage from a stolen password
supporting: Caller ID and sender addresses are easily spoofed, especially over VoIP
Where to report in the U.S.: ReportFraud.ftc.gov; forward texts to SPAM (7726); forward emails to APWG (reportphishing@apwg.org)
IdentityTheft.gov for recovery if credentials or financial data were surrendered
Hovering over a link reveals whether its true destination matches the visible text
outOfScope: Malware internals and types (owned by computer-literacy:foundations:malware) — noted only as a phishing payload
Password construction and MFA setup depth (owned by password-security / MFA topics) — referenced only
Any attacker instructions, phishing-kit construction, or offensive techniques — deliberately excluded

claims.claim: Phishing occurs when criminals try to get people to open harmful links, emails, or attachments, or to reveal personal or financial information, via a message designed to look like it comes from a trusted person or organization; it arrives as email, text, social-media direct message, or phone call.
Phishing is a form of social engineering, in which an attacker uses human interaction to obtain or compromise information rather than defeating technical controls.

Common red flags include urgent or emotionally appealing language claiming dire consequences for not responding immediately, requests to send personal or financial information, untrusted shortened URLs, and incorrect/lookalike email addresses or links (e.g., amazan.com).
Poor grammar and spelling used to be a common sign, but in the era of AI some phishing emails now have perfect grammar and spelling, so recipients should look for the other signs.

Additional phishing indicators include generic greetings such as 'Dear Valued Customer', spoofed hyperlinks whose true destination does not match the visible text, unexpected attachments used to deliver malware, unrecognized/fake invoices, and offers of free items or refunds that are not real.
Spear phishing is a highly targeted phishing attack aimed at a specific individual or organization.
Whaling is a specific kind of phishing that targets high-ranking members of organizations (e.g., executives).
Smishing is phishing that exploits SMS or text messages; vishing is phishing that leverages voice communication, and VoIP makes caller ID easy to spoof.

If a message could be real, do not click any link or call any number in it; instead find another way to contact the company or person directly (go to the verified website yourself, or use a number you already have) to confirm.

The recommended response is to recognize, resist (don't click links or attachments, don't reply, including 'unsubscribe' links), report the phishing (to the company, via a 'report spam' option, or to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov; forward phishing texts to SPAM/7726 and emails to APWG at reportphishing@apwg.org), and delete the message.
Multifactor authentication requires more than a password to access an account and helps prevent others from logging in even if they obtain the password.
If you think a scammer has your Social Security, credit card, or bank account information, go to IdentityTheft.gov for the specific steps to take.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether spelling/grammar errors are a reliable phishing indicator.
positions: Traditional guidance lists poor grammar and misspellings as a red flag.
CISA (current Secure Our World guidance) notes AI now enables perfect grammar, so its absence does not indicate legitimacy.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented both: grammar errors remain a possible sign, but the lesson stresses that clean grammar is no longer reassurance and readers should rely on the other, more durable signs (requests, links, sender, urgency).

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Phishing is a foundational concept... a simple way to apply it') with no substantive, sourced claims about phishing at all.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire boilerplate draft with substantive, sourced content: an actual definition, red flags, named variants, response/reporting steps, and the MFA mitigation.
Added the current-guidance caveat that AI-generated phishing can have perfect grammar.
Populated real vocabulary definitions (draft's vocabulary was circular, e.g., defining phishing as 'a foundational Computer Literacy concept covered in this lesson').
rightsIssues: All five sources are U.S. federal government works (CISA, FTC, NIST), which are in the public domain. Content was nonetheless synthesized into original prose; no source wording was reproduced beyond short factual phrases in evidence notes.
Content is strictly recognition and defense; no attack instructions, phishing-kit techniques, or offensive code are included, per subject cautions.

sourceRecords.title: Recognize and Report Phishing
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. government guidance (public domain). Supports the definition (harmful links/attachments or requests for personal/financial info via messages impersonating a trusted party, arriving by email/text/DM/phone), the recognize-resist-delete response, the red flags (urgency, requests for information, shortened URLs, lookalike addresses like amazan.com), the current note that AI enables perfect grammar, the verify-through-a-known-channel advice, and the strong-passwords/MFA safety net. sourceRecords.title: How To Recognize and Avoid Phishing Scams
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. government consumer guidance (public domain). Supports the phishing tactics list (fake suspicious-activity/account-problem claims, requests to confirm personal/financial info, fake invoices, malicious payment links, fake refunds and free-stuff offers), the generic-greeting sign, the four protections (security software with auto-updates, phone auto-updates, MFA, backups), what to do (verify with a known number/website, don't click), how to report (ReportFraud.ftc.gov; forward texts to SPAM/7726; emails to reportphishing@apwg.org), and IdentityTheft.gov for recovery. Read 2026-08-19 via curl with a browser user-agent following the redirect from the older /how-recognize-and-avoid-phishing-scams URL.

sourceRecords.title: Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks (ST04-014)
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. government guidance (public domain). Supports phishing as a form of social engineering, the vishing definition (voice communication; VoIP allows caller ID to be spoofed), the smishing definition (exploits SMS/text messages), and the common phishing indicators (suspicious sender address imitating a legitimate business, generic greetings and signature, spoofed hyperlinks/websites and lookalike or shortened URLs, spelling/layout problems, suspicious attachments as a malware delivery mechanism). Read 2026-08-19 via curl with a browser user-agent.
